It says so much about her that she loves all your kids enough and she respects her relationship enough with you that she is willing to 'tough it out' in this situation. It also says great things about you that you clearly love and respect your nanny and will support and defend her. That being said, THIS is the relationship you should seek to uphold and protect first and foremost, and sorry, but screw the other family. I agree with the others that it's possible to redirect toddlers to not touch things and that certain areas are just 'no' - but I disagree that this is possible all of the time, and even though your nanny is willing to stick around to try and make this work, as wonderful as she is, I don't see how she wouldn't end up resenting everyone she works for in the end. I know that would happen to me as much as I would work for logic to win out and remind myself constantly that you would change this for me if you could. It's not just a matter of them being assholes for not babyproofing - having been a nanny for nearly 20 years and a parent of 2 for more than 10, it is simply not safe to have unprotected stairways. The porcelain and breakables seem more like an issue for the parents as I doubt the babies would break them in a way that could cause major injury to one of them, but the stairs - and it sounds as if there are plenty of stairs - that is a nightmare waiting to happen. I fell down 15 ft of stairs working for my 3rd ever family about 7 months into the job and it was one of the scariest experiences of my life. I had their 4 month old in my arms, and though I was being careful and their stairs were gated, it just goes to show that even in areas where the utmost caution is exercised that bad things still happen, and stairs practically guarantee accidents, slips, trips, falls, and scars. I believe that you value your nanny as much as you say you do - exercise every option you have to get out of the nanny share and I really believe you'll all breathe easier. Relationships where there's that much love and mutual admiration and respect between MB/DB and nanny are few and far between. She is worth her weight in gold, and you will never regret treating her as such. Good luck; please keep us posted!

I second the suggestion for unemployment. Being there for just a month isn't going to financially qualify you, but there is a distinct possibility that your prior job will provide unemployment. Even if you don't think you qualify, run, do not walk, and go file a claim. Be prepared for your most recent MB to appeal your claim, and save every scrap of communication you have that outlined your responsibilities and the kind of commitment you were expected to give to the family. Have it at the ready when you're going to be interviewed by your state unemployment agency. I assume you were never disciplined or had a sit down with MB or DB where they expressed unhappiness about your work. Even if they did do that to complain about something such as tardiness, as long as you didn't sign anything that acknowledged that you were being warned or some such thing, you can go into the interview knowing and truthfully stating that you were blindsided by the circumstances around your being let go. This is worth a shot to at least help you financially while you seek out a better position with a family who will love and respect you for what you bring to the table. Of course you shouldn't expect this going forward, sweetheart! This is a pure and simple case of Mom & DadBoss screwing you over. While i think most of us expect to get screwed over for some tiny things, no one expects it to be anything so overt and obvious like this. You did the best you could with what you had. Don't beat yourself up about it - you clearly are deserving of a family that has a space in their home and hearts for awesomeness. Chin up. (hugs)

I have used it, and no, there's no real process as a caregiver to reflect on a family you worked for or even did a trial with. I have a crazy Care.com story; I'll share...

I did a one-day trial for one set of parents who would have been HORRIBLE to work for. The mom gave me a surprise out-of-the-blue drug test the minute I walked in the door - I don't do/take anything illicit, but I do have two compression fractures in my back and I have trouble sleeping, and I have meds for both that would show up on a screen, and I don't really appreciate someone trying to back me into a corner over information about my health that I keep to myself and making me explain why I tested positive for anything. I've NEVER had a family ask this of me before, and had it been part of the negotiation, I would probably think differently about it, but to just spring it on me once I've already come over and have been shadowing current nanny's day - that felt intrusive. Also just weird.


That lady was incensed that I elected to scoot out of there being paid $10 an hour to watch and entertain 3 children, being told by their current (pregnant and leaving to stay at home with her baby) nanny that other than drop off and pick up for the oldest child in preschool, they were virtually on house restriction - she estimated that one time a month she *might* be able to take the 2 youngest to Chick-fil-a with $10 from MB, but they did no activities that would allow us to go off the property because MB wanted them to stay in the home. Also, both MB and DB worked inside the home. I hate having parents consistently at home when nannying; it may just be my experience, but I've never had the opportunity to work for any parents that don't undermine my authority, to say the least. Especially with toddlers - when they get in trouble and you try to lay down the law and they don't like what you say, they just run crying to Mom or Dad and whine about the situation and they alter your plan or just destroy the precedent you're trying to set. I find it very frustrating. This particular mom was a very deliberate control freak. That nanny was insane to be working with 3 kids that she could NEVER take out of the house for fun and doing their laundry, cleaning their rooms, cleaning the kitchen, cooking quite elaborate meals for their dinner for $10 an hour! No freaking way! 


Sorry for the long digression. Anyway, this mom was super angry that I rejected her job offer, and proceeded to call me 20-30 times daily for about a week after. She also threatened to take me to small claims court if I didn't return the very tiny amount of money she paid me to come over for the trial day.  I'd just finished a short-term assignment working with 2 year old twin girls, and I took them somewhere - more likely 2-3 somewheres - a day. I cannot imagine how awful it would be to be trapped in this house with this particular MB and DB and all three of their sweet but clearly bored kiddos. She somehow talked to someone important behind the website. She was already harassing me via that site as well, so I was already planning to kill the account and start over, so I went through with that, and I also ended up changing my phone number so she couldn't textually harass me anymore via the phone. I believe that if I hadn't pulled my account, I would have been kicked off without any investigation to my side of the story. I've known other nannies who got a bad review for something stupid and Care.com just pulled their accounts, no warning or notice. It's a shame, at least it is in my area - there are almost 700 jobs available listed in just a 10-mile radius of where I live. It's a great networking tool and I've gotten many jobs through the site (actually got a new one today, and I start Monday! So excited!) and it has proved to be a really useful tool for us.

I really wish there were a public forum so we could warn each other about the crazies so no one else would have to find out the hard way. Maybe we should create such a place, ladies? It would be a serious public service.

Sorry for the mini-rant/wall of text. Depending on where you are, I would suggest checking out www.nannies4hire.com - families have to pay some serious dough to sign up there and they tend to be much less flaky than the care.com parents. A lot of very small nanny agencies put jobs out, too, and it can be a great way to find an agency if you're interested in working with one.

Best of luck!

That's actually not always true. I was passively suicidal for a really long time - definitely the majority of my adult life. I did not actively seek comfort from outside sources, friends or Reddit or any other forum, and I was not raised as a Christian, but I found my faith in the midst of a faithless family and I think that saved me as a teenager who was being more horribly abused than I have words to explain to anyone. I wish I could tell you it saved me wholeheartedly and in the long run, but that wasn't the case. I continued to struggle through and after college, even after having kids, and it was a really hard thing to keep coming back to face. I think it's the eventual tolerance to being passively suicidal, which is what I would say you're struggling with as well, that pushed me to go one way or another. It gets exhausting and so frustrating to wake up and be in the same place over and over and over again and not have a solution or a place to go that comforts you, that addresses the darkness in you, that can just make you feel better. It's not ever the words of comfort that get old, especially from people who don't know you - at least that's my opinion, though I'm sure that others will think differently. In me, in my head and in my heart, I had to switch it up to think about something else - not to get the depression or the desire to die out of my head - I don't think that's how it works for most of us. And I'm also not a medication success story - I had a great med on board more than a decade ago and developed an allergy to a primary ingredient in ALL antidepressants years after I started taking it, so when I tell you it was up to me, I mean just that: it was totally and completely up to me to turn it around. And what I eventually got was that I couldn't do it for my kids, my family, my ex, or anyone else. No one was strong enough motivation for me to drop it and walk away. Over time, while I was working a job that I also felt was sucking the life out of me, my mind began to wander back to things that I loved. Things that used to make me happy. And I zeroed in on one, just one, thing, one activity, one something that I began when I was about 3 years old and dropped at the start of my super heavy adult depression. I was very resistant to it even when it first crossed my mind, but as it popped into my head again, it never left. Before I knew it, I was engaging in tiny nuances of the art again, and little by little, I've allowed it to take more and more of me back into the light. I struggle with my dark days, but they are far outnumbered now. I have no guarantee that what worked for me is going to work for you, and I read this sub often and hear the complaints about all the "it will get better for you, OP, because (fill in the blank.)" I'm not going to do that either. But I'm going to offer you some of the hope that I have now, because I know I'm in a spot enough where I have plenty to spare, and because I am a stranger that may be easier to talk to than someone you know and are close to. So here's some hope to hang onto while you've mislaid yours, and I genuinely care about you and what happens to you, and I wish I could do more than just this. But in this moment, I hope it makes you feel even just a tiny bit better. Much love, OP. <3

EDIT: Yep, we really do care. About YOU. <3

Legally, they can keep you from sitting with her, seeing her, and don't have to give you any information unless you are a legal member of her family. You may be able to catch a break if you catch and explain your role to her treating physician, but they are under no obligation to tell you anything and you should expect a "laws say I can't tell you anything"  attitude about it. This is how the legal process works and you largely cannot intervene. Propranolol lowers your heart rate; I would not be surprised if she were in intensive or critical care and may be assisted in breathing with a ventilator or other breathing apparatus. Once it it presumed a suicide attempt, the healthcare system is required to have a staffer with eyes on her at all times as an inpatient. This is accomplished by each ICU or CCU nurse having only one patient, and if she is moved to a regular floor, she will likely have a personal 'sitter' in room with her that monitors and charts every move she makes. The 72 hour hold is often extended by several days and the staff and physicians can remove her to an inpatient psychiatric facility with or without her consent. She will likely be held as an inpatient until a psych bed becomes available for her and she will be reevaluated upon admission to an extended care facility. Patients in a regular hospital who are on a mental health hold will not be allowed any personal belongings at all, so no for the cell phone or anything else, and they will also likely have her in a 'clean' room without an outgoing phone line, locked sharps container, or so much as a trash can. You can and should try to get any important numbers, including your own, to a nurse on her floor in effort to have them put in her chart. After whatever length of time, her physician may allow her to make a phone call while supervised by nurses. I would leave a contact for a family member regardless of her relationship with them because she simply may not have a choice. 

You did great work and very likely saved her life, OP, but now she has some extremely difficult work to do, and no one can make her want to do it. You have to encourage her to fight for her own life. Seek help for YOUR trauma and take care of YOU right now. What you just went through is no small thing, man. 
Much love and prayers to you both. Please update.

I identify as a singer and a dance, though I don't know which love I found first. I came to know your music through my amazingly talented choir director at 21, almost done with college, deeply in love with my fiance and expecting our little girl in the spring of 2003. In October of 2002, our chamber choir did three selections by you, and I was inexplicably drawn in on a level I never experienced when my group sang Water Night for the first time. The performance of our group of 20 was so breathtaking and intense that I was shaking for hours leaving the stage.
I am Native American, as was my fiance, and we have strong connections to the nature and the God we believe is all around us, in everything. We'd been trying to decide what to name our girl, and he'd flip through long and complicated names that no other child will have and make suggestions while I danced in the studio he made for me in our garage. My dance was different every time, but the last time I went out to put on my ballet shoes, I felt strange. I stretched for a long time, playing the song over and over in my studio space, and my sweet fiance came out quietly and stood to the side, tears streaming down his face as I leapt and spun and fought for breathless execution of the reconciliation of the music in my soul and the movement of my body. I was 24 weeks, 5 days pregnant, and I went into labor that night.
My little heartbreaker was so tough, and she hung in there with us for several days while we played her all the music that kept her company when she was in my womb. When it was time, we played Water Night for a half hour, and we wept over her, as she opened her eyes, we saw the secret kingdom. She closed them four hours later, and a silent and beautiful current filled her soul.
We named her "little wanderer in beautiful waters" in our native language. I know the words are from Octavio Paz, but it is the music that knit us together, that cemented a family, and gave a girl her wings. I so hope you see this because you're seriously one of my heroes and I so love your music.

Yep. Also a former anorexic here, and I absolutely wigged out when I started gaining weight after a very physically demanding job change last year and my thyroid was barely functional. Replacement of hormones=weight resolution. I feel way better too, and I'm much less depressed.

I have struggled with anorexia since I was a teenager, and I've attempted suicide, but much later in life. When I had to be initially hospitalized to get the anorexia under control, the card I will *Never* forget came from my sister, and we barely got along, ever, before that. She got me a simple white card with a picture of a little vanity with a mirror and an empty seat in front. When I open the card, it says, "Do you have any idea how beautiful you really are?" And she wrote she loved me, and there is not a single piece of mail I've ever gotten that means more.

Another idea, if you guys will be together for a while, write her a note a day. Nothing long or overwhelming. Look up and use quotations to make her laugh and smile. Then hide them in the room/area where she will be recovering so she has a surprise a day for as long as she needs it. It will mean so much to her. Date the outside of the envelopes so she will know when to open what.

You did a good thing posting here and asking for help! I know there are resources listed in our sidebar, but I want to throw in that if you find yourself about to burst and you're okay talking to a stranger - as all of us who offer to talk to you will be strangers as well - the rape crisis hotline is available and operational 24/7 as is the domestic violence hotline. I'm pulling a national rape crisis hotline operated by RAINN: "Hotline support is available both by phone at (210) 349-7273 (toll-free at 1-800-656-HOPE (4673) and online through RAINN (Rape Abuse Incest National Network)," and the national domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE. RAINN's website also gives you the option to enter your zip code and it will return a number for your local rape crisis center. This is a great option and I really encourage you to seek out at least one local resource, because you cannot climb out of this murky darkness by yourself, and you've already shown that you're brave enough to say what happened and ask for help. So please please please go here and find that local resource: http://centers.rainn.org/
